newsitem.title: UK: Low British unemployment not set to fuel inflation.
newsitem.headline: Low British unemployment not set to fuel inflation.

text.p: Britain's jobless queues could fall by another 500,000 without fuelling inflationary pressures as long as the recent rapid cut in unemployment tailed off, the Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) said on Wednesday.
In a separate survey, the Trades Union Congress said many of the jobs on offer were low paid and part-time.

Professor Douglas McWilliams, chief executive of the CEBR economic consultancy, said unemployment was currently falling "dangerously fast" and forecast the jobless rate could drop to five percent from 6.9 now.
Jobless numbers are currently being cut by about 40,000 people a month.

"This is too rapid. If unemployment continued to fall at this pace it would lead to inflationary pressures and to higher interest rates, which would in turn eventually bring the falls in unemployment to an end," he said.

A sustainable pace of decline would see the jobless total fall by 10,000 a month. "This would be a pace of decline that would be consistent with inflation staying low and hence with a sustained reduction in unemployment."

Official unemployment figures are due out at 0930 GMT on Wednesday. A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus forecast that British unemployment fell by 30,000 in December, following a record drop of 96,000 the month before.
One of the reasons that rapidly falling unemployment is not sparking price pressures could be that many of the jobs on offer pay very low wages.
The TUC, an umbrella body for trades unions, said while jobs were being created, vacancies at job centres were mainly for poorly paid work with some paying less than one pound ($1.67) an hour.
The report showed almost half the vacancies surveyed paid less than 3.70 pounds an hour, with the lowest rate at 74 pence an hour for a nanny.
More than 5,000 jobs surveyed in England and Wales paid an average weekly wage of 168.90 pounds for a full-time job, almost half the national average.
Nearly a third paid less than 61 pounds a week and one in three vacancies were part-time, according to the survey by the TUC Unemployed Centres.
On top of that, one in 10 jobs on offer were for more than 48 hours a week, in contravention of European Union rules on maximum working hours.

TUC general secretary John Monks said: "The survey shows that the jobs on offer are likely to be low paid and part-time. Many of the full-time jobs pay so little that people will have to do excessive hours just to receive a living wage." ($1=.5979 Stg)
